name: Wrangler
summary: The command-line tool for Cloudflare Workers: it reads `wrangler.jsonc`, runs your Worker locally on the real runtime, deploys it, and manages the D1, KV, R2 and other resources it binds to.
intro: Wrangler is an npm package you install into each project, so a team pins one version. Its config file, `wrangler.jsonc` (recommended for new projects; `wrangler.toml` still works), names the Worker, its entry point, a `compatibility_date` that fixes runtime behavior, routes, per-environment overrides and every binding: KV namespaces, R2 buckets, D1 databases, Durable Objects, Queues, secrets. Cloudflare treats this file as the source of truth for a Worker’s configuration.

`wrangler dev` runs your Worker on your machine through Miniflare, which hosts it in `workerd`, the same runtime as production. Bindings point at local simulations that start empty, unless you mark one `remote: true` to reach the real resource while the code still runs locally. `wrangler deploy` bundles the code with esbuild, then uploads and activates a version; `versions upload` and `versions deploy` split that into two steps, and `rollback`, `tail` (a live log session), `secret put` and `types` (generates `Env` types from your bindings) cover the rest of the loop. Subcommands such as `d1`, `kv`, `r2`, `queues`, `hyperdrive`, `vectorize` and `secrets-store` manage resources; since v4 they act on local data unless you pass `--remote`.
strengths: Local development runs the production runtime, not an imitation: Cloudflare measured 10x faster startup and 60x faster reloads than the old remote mode
One tool and one config file for code, bindings, environments, secrets and most Developer Platform resources
Per-binding `remote: true` lets you test local code against real data without deploying
Open source under MIT or Apache 2.0, and installed per project so CI and laptops use the same version
limits: Needs a supported Node.js release (Current, Active or Maintenance LTS) and, via `workerd`, macOS 13.5+, Windows 11 or a Linux with glibc 2.35+
Local simulations start empty and differ from production data; Workers AI always runs remotely, and Durable Objects and Workflows can’t be remote bindings
Since v4, `kv` and `r2` commands default to local storage, so old scripts silently stop touching production until you add `--remote`
Some newer features work only with a JSON config file, so older `wrangler.toml` projects may need converting

worksWith.how: creates, migrates and queries databases in
creates buckets and uploads objects to

snippet.title: The everyday loop
source: npm i -D wrangler@4                     # installed per project
npx wrangler dev                        # local server on workerd via Miniflare
npx wrangler types                      # generate Env types from your bindings
npx wrangler d1 execute my-db --local  --command "SELECT count(*) FROM users"
npx wrangler d1 execute my-db --remote --command "SELECT count(*) FROM users"
npx wrangler secret put STRIPE_KEY      # prompts for the value, deploys a new version
npx wrangler deploy                     # upload and activate
npx wrangler tail                       # live log session for the deployed Worker

story: On March 28, 2019, Ashley Williams open-sourced the first `wrangler`, written in Rust and installed with `cargo install`, as “just enough” tooling to build, preview and publish Workers written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. Its later `wrangler dev` command ran your code on Cloudflare’s network, and every change took a few seconds to show up.

On November 16, 2021, Ashcon Partovi and Sunil Pai announced wrangler 2.0, a new generation with zero-config `wrangler dev`, a Chrome DevTools debugger and a switch to “local mode” powered by Miniflare, a Node.js simulator created by Brendan Coll that had just joined the Cloudflare organization. Version 2.0.0 shipped on npm in May 2022. Local mode reimplemented the runtime in JavaScript, so it never behaved exactly like production.

That changed after Cloudflare open-sourced the real runtime, `workerd`, in 2022. Wrangler v3, released on May 17, 2023, made local development the default, running Miniflare 3 on `workerd`. Wrangler v4 followed on March 13, 2025 with a smaller set of changes: a newer esbuild, Node.js 16 dropped, and resource commands that default to local. Wrangler now lives in the `workers-sdk` monorepo with Miniflare and `create-cloudflare`.

choices.why: Remote development was slow to start and reload and billed KV and R2 operations. Running `workerd` locally gave production behavior with 10x faster startup and 60x faster reloads, with `--remote` kept for real data.
`workerd` provides the runtime and bindings but not the storage behind them, so Miniflare supplies local KV, R2, D1, Queues and Cache backed by SQLite.
A team then shares one Wrangler version, can pin it per project and roll back if a release breaks something.

timeline.text: First `wrangler` open-sourced on March 28, a Rust CLI for Rust and WebAssembly Workers
wrangler 2.0 beta on November 16, with local mode via Miniflare
wrangler 2.0.0 released on npm in May
Wrangler v3 on May 17 makes `workerd`-based local development the default
Wrangler v4 on March 13; commands default to local data
